blocks.text: Multiple-choice questions in the same format as Devmaxx, with full explanations for every option. Use this as a **diagnostic**: answer first, then read the explanation. If you get one wrong, go back to the referenced chapter. **Scoring yourself:** 90%+ = senior ready. 75-89% = strong mid. 60-74% = good foundation, go back and re-read. Below 60% = restart from [Ch. 00](00-foundations.md).

**Q1. You cache API responses. Reads dominate; data updates every 5 minutes. What's the right invalidation strategy?** A. TTL-based expiration B. Write-through cache, no expiry C. No caching, hit the DB every time D. Manual purge on every request
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**A. TTL-based expiration.** The data's staleness tolerance is 5 minutes, so a 5-minute TTL directly encodes the business requirement. B is wrong: "no expiry" means a value can be stale forever if an invalidation is ever missed — and write-through still needs a TTL as a safety net. C trades a huge performance win for nothing. D ("manual purge on every request") is self-defeating — you'd purge on every read, so the hit rate would be ~0.
Related: [Ch. 06](06-caching.md) §3, §5. </details>

**Q2. Which cache pathology describes: 10,000 keys all expire at exactly midnight, and the database receives 100% of traffic?** A. Cache penetration B. Cache avalanche C. Cache stampede D. Cache breakdown
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B. Cache avalanche.** Many keys expiring simultaneously. Fix: jitter the TTLs so expiry times spread out, plus stale-while-revalidate to serve stale during refills.

items.text: **Penetration** = requests for keys that don't exist, so every one misses.
**Stampede** = many concurrent requests for *one* hot key that just expired.
**Breakdown** = the cache itself goes down and the origin is overwhelmed.

blocks.text: Related: [Ch. 06](06-caching.md) §6. </details>

**Q3. A hot key expires and 5,000 concurrent requests all miss the cache and hit the database. What's the best fix?** A. Increase the TTL B. Use a longer cache key prefix C. Request coalescing (single-flight) D. Add a second Redis instance
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**C. Request coalescing (single-flight).** Only one request populates the cache; the rest wait for its result. This directly eliminates the herd. A longer TTL reduces the *frequency* of expiry but doesn't fix the herd when it happens. D spreads the load but doesn't stop the duplicate work.
Alternatives: refresh-ahead, stale-while-revalidate, probabilistic early expiration (XFetch).
Related: [Ch. 06](06-caching.md) §6. </details>

**Q4. Which statement about write-behind (write-back) caching is true?** A. It's the fastest way to read data B. It can lose committed writes if the cache dies before the async write lands C. It guarantees strong consistency D. It eliminates cache invalidation problems
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Write-behind updates the cache synchronously and the origin asynchronously, so a cache crash in that window loses data that was already acknowledged. It's only acceptable for reproducible or tolerant data, and only with a durable cache. A is wrong — write-behind speeds up *writes*, not reads. C is backwards. D is wrong — write-behind creates a *new* problem (drift between cache and origin) rather than removing invalidation.
Related: [Ch. 06](06-caching.md) §3. </details>

**Q5. Why is `Vary: Cookie` dangerous on a CDN?** A. It disables HTTPS B. Each distinct cookie value creates a separate cache entry, collapsing the hit rate C. It prevents range requests D. It forces a full revalidation on every request
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** The cache key includes the cookie value, so with millions of users the CDN stores millions of near-duplicate entries and almost every request is a miss — which means the origin takes the full load and the CDN bill goes up. The fix is `Cache-Control: private` for personalized content, or personalize *after* the cache lookup (cached shell, dynamic hole).
Related: [Ch. 11](11-cdn.md) §2. </details>

**Q6. What is the primary benefit of making application servers stateless?** A. It reduces memory usage per instance B. Any instance can serve any request, enabling horizontal scaling and rolling deploys C. It eliminates the need for a load balancer D. It guarantees strong consistency
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Statelessness makes instances interchangeable → you can add/remove them freely, autoscale safely, and deploy with zero downtime. A is a side effect, not the point. C and D are unrelated.
Related: [Ch. 01](01-scaling.md) §2. </details>

**Q7. A service is IO-bound: CPU sits at 12% but p99 latency is climbing. What's the best autoscaling signal?** A. CPU utilization B. In-flight request concurrency C. Memory usage D. p99 latency alone
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** The instance is saturated on connections, not CPU — CPU looks idle while every worker is blocked on IO. Scaling on CPU would under-provision. D alone oscillates (latency is a lagging indicator); pair it with concurrency.
Related: [Ch. 01](01-scaling.md) §4. </details>

**Q8. Why must a liveness probe NOT check the database?** A. Databases don't expose health endpoints B. A database blip would fail every instance at once, restarting the entire fleet and escalating the outage C. Liveness probes are too expensive to run frequently D. It would break the readiness probe
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** This is the classic thundering-herd restart: a 30-second DB hiccup → every instance fails liveness → all restart simultaneously → cold caches → a surge of connections at a cold DB → longer outage. Liveness should test only the process; dependency checks belong in **readiness** (remove from the load balancer, don't restart).
Related: [Ch. 01](01-scaling.md) §3, [Ch. 15](15-reliability.md) §3.2. </details>
**Q9. You have 20 instances, each enforcing "100 requests/second" locally. What's the effective global limit?** A. 100 rps B. 2,000 rps C. 20 rps D. Unbounded
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Per-instance limits multiply. Worse, the effective per-user limit is unpredictable because distribution across instances is uneven. To get a true global limit you need shared state (Redis) or to divide by the instance count — and instance count changes with autoscaling.
Related: [Ch. 10](10-rate-limiting.md) §4. </details>

**Q10. What's the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing?** A. L4 is faster but can't route by URL or terminate TLS B. L7 is more secure C. L4 only supports HTTP D. L7 cannot perform health checks
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**A.** L4 balances TCP connections using IP:port only — cheap and fast, but no URL routing, no caching, no HTTP-aware health checks. L7 understands HTTP and can route by path/header, cache, terminate TLS, and return 503 for unhealthy backends. L4 is what you'd use for raw TCP/UDP (databases) or internal traffic; L7 for public HTTP APIs.
Related: [Ch. 01](01-scaling.md) §3. </details>

**Q11. Which query does the index `(tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)` support?** A. `WHERE status = ?` B. `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC` C. `WHERE created_at < ?` D. `WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ?`
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B** only. A composite index is usable only with the **leading** column in the predicate. A and D skip `tenant_id`, so the index can't be used for the lookup. C also skips the leading column.
Rule of thumb for column order: **equality filters first, then range, then sort.**
Related: [Ch. 02](02-databases.md) §3. </details>

**Q12. What is the N+1 problem?** A. Querying the same table twice in one transaction B. One query to fetch a list, then one additional query per item for related data C. A deadlock between two concurrent transactions D. An index that isn't used by the query planner
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Fixes: a JOIN (one query), a batch/DataLoader (`WHERE id IN (...)`), or denormalizing the child summary into the parent. It's the most common performance bug in application code.
Related: [Ch. 02](02-databases.md) §3. </details>

**Q13. Two transactions both read a balance of 100 and both write 90. What happened, and what's the fix?** A. A dirty read; use serializable isolation B. A lost update; use an atomic `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 10` C. A phantom read; use snapshot isolation D. Write skew; use a constraint
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** This is a **lost update** — $10 vanished. The canonical fix is making the write atomic (`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = ?`), which the DB serializes. Alternatives: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, optimistic concurrency with a version column, or routing all writes for an account to a single owner.
Related: [Ch. 02](02-databases.md) §4. </details>

**Q14. You're building a ride-sharing app. Which datastore is the right default?** A. Cassandra, because ride data is high-volume B. MongoDB, because trips are nested documents C. Postgres, because the data is relational and you need transactions for payments D. Redis, for speed
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**C.** The data is relational (users, drivers, trips, payments) and you need transactions for money. Postgres handles 10–50k writes/sec with proper indexing — you almost certainly don't need a distributed store. Reach for Cassandra only when a *measured* write limit or access pattern demands it, and note that each additional datastore is a consistency boundary and an operational burden.
Related: [Ch. 02](02-databases.md) §1. </details>

**Q15. Which statement about embedding vs. referencing in a document store is correct?** A. Always embed — it avoids joins B. Always reference — it keeps documents small C. Embed when the child is bounded and always read with the parent; reference when unbounded D. It doesn't matter as long as you index correctly
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**C.** The classic fatal mistake is embedding an *unbounded* array (e.g. all post IDs in a user document) — it grows until it hits the 16 MB document limit and slows every read. Embed bounded children read with the parent; reference unbounded or independently-accessed ones.
Related: [Ch. 02](02-databases.md) §5. </details>

**Q16. Why does `hash(key) % N` make reshardding painful?** A. It's too slow to compute B. Changing N remaps nearly every key, requiring a full data migration C. It produces uneven distribution D. It doesn't support range queries
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Adding one server to N=1000 changes the modulo for ~all 1B keys. Consistent hashing fixes this by ensuring only ~1/N of keys move. (C and D are also true of modulo hashing, but B is the reason consistent hashing exists.)
Related: [Ch. 03](03-sharding.md) §3. </details>

**Q17. What's the purpose of virtual nodes in consistent hashing?** A. To store metadata about the cluster B. To even out key distribution and make server removal move only ~1/N of the data C. To reduce the number of hash functions D. To replicate data across nodes
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** With one ring point per server, gaps are unevenly sized and the distribution is noisy. 100+ vnodes per server smooths the distribution and makes removal of one server move only that server's ~1/N share rather than an arbitrary large slice.
Related: [Ch. 03](03-sharding.md) §3. </details>

**Q18. You shard by `country`. What happens during a soccer final?** A. Nothing — the algorithm handles it B. The host country's shard becomes a hot shard C. The hash ring rebalances automatically D. Writes to other countries fail
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Country has low cardinality and highly skewed traffic — the classic hot shard. This is exactly why the shard key should have high cardinality and low skew, and why it should be chosen around your hottest query's co-location needs, not around a convenient attribute.
Related: [Ch. 03](03-sharding.md) §2. </details>

**Q19. Why might you choose NOT to shard, even at high traffic?** A. Sharding is always the right answer at scale B. The bottleneck isn't the database, sharding is operationally expensive and hard to reverse, and a single well-tuned Postgres may be enough C. Sharding doesn't support transactions D. Sharding requires microservices
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Sharding is a *reactive* decision. If the real bottleneck is CPU, network, or an external API, sharding solves nothing while adding enormous operational complexity and an irreversible migration. Confirm the bottleneck first.
Related: [Ch. 03](03-sharding.md) §2, [Ch. 18](18-design-playbook.md) §6. </details>

**Q20. What's the transactional outbox pattern?** A. Write to two databases for redundancy B. Write the business data and an event row in one local transaction; a relay publishes the event C. Buffer writes in memory and flush them nightly D. A Kafka feature for exactly-once delivery
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** It eliminates the **dual-write failure**: without it, the DB write can succeed while the message publish fails, permanently desynchronizing state and events. With it, the event is published *at least once*, and idempotent consumers make the effect exactly-once.
Related: [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md) §6, [Ch. 07](07-message-queues.md) §10. </details>

**Q21. What does synchronous replication cost you that asynchronous replication doesn't?** A. Storage cost B. A network round trip per write, plus coupling write availability to the replica's health C. The ability to read from replicas D. Backup capability
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Synchronous replication adds 1 ms (same region) or 50–150 ms (cross-region) to every write and means a slow replica can stall all writes. What it buys is a **zero data-loss window** (RPO ≈ 0) for acknowledged writes.
Related: [Ch. 04](04-replication.md) §3. </details>

**Q22. A user updates their profile then immediately reloads and sees the old value. What's the cause?** A. Read-your-writes violation from replica lag B. A failed cache invalidation C. A lost update D. Clock skew
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**A.** The read hit a replica that hadn't applied the write yet. Fixes: route that session's reads to the primary for N seconds; return an LSN/version token with the write and have the read wait for or route to a caught-up replica; or don't read from replicas for correctness-critical reads.
Related: [Ch. 04](04-replication.md) §5. </details>

**Q23. Why is a failed ping insufficient to declare a primary dead?** A. Pings can be spoofed B. Network failures are asymmetric — the primary may still reach the replicas C. Pings are too slow D. Replicas can't receive pings
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** The primary might be talking to the replicas while they can't reach it. Promoting on a ping failure creates **split brain**. You need a **quorum** decision, or a lease expiry plus fencing, before declaring failure.
Related: [Ch. 04](04-replication.md) §6, [Ch. 08](08-distributed-primitives.md) §9. </details>

**Q24. What is a fencing token, and what does it prevent?** A. A random nonce that identifies the lock holder B. A monotonically increasing token issued per lock acquisition; the resource rejects writes with a stale token C. A TTL that expires the lock D. A hash of the resource name
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** A lease alone isn't enough: the holder can stall past its expiry and resume writing concurrently with the new holder. A fencing token makes the **resource** reject the stale holder's writes, so exclusivity holds even when the old holder believes it still owns the lock.
Related: [Ch. 08](08-distributed-primitives.md) §5.3. </details>

**Q25. Why is a replica not a backup?** A. Replicas are slower B. A replica faithfully copies deletions and corruption; you still need point-in-time backups C. Replicas aren't encrypted D. Replicas don't support the same queries
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Restoring a replica restores the damage. You need snapshots + WAL/binlog archiving (PITR), stored separately, and you must **test restores**.
Related: [Ch. 04](04-replication.md) §1, [Ch. 15](15-reliability.md) §6. </details>

**Q26. State CAP correctly.** A. Pick any two of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance B. During a partition, you must choose between consistency and availability; partition tolerance is mandatory C. CAP only applies to microservices D. CAP means you must always be available
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** The common "pick 2 of 3" phrasing is a misreading. Partitions always happen, so P is required; during one, you choose C (block/reject, e.g. Postgres primary-replica) or A (serve stale, e.g. Cassandra). PACELC adds the else-branch: even without a partition you trade consistency for latency on every request.
Related: [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md) §2. </details>
**Q27. With N=3 replicas, W=2, R=2 — is a stale read possible?** A. Yes B. No, because W + R > N C. Yes, but only during a partition D. Only if one replica is corrupted
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** The write is on ≥2 of 3 replicas, so at most 1 lacks it. A read of 2 replicas can only miss the write if *both* lack it — impossible. The rule is **W + R > N** guarantees quorum overlap.
Contrast: W=2, R=1 → 2+1 = 3, not > 3 → a read can hit the one stale replica and return an old value. That's the classic misconfiguration.
Related: [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md) §4. </details>

**Q28. What does idempotency mean and why does it matter?** A. Operations that complete within a fixed time B. Applying an operation multiple times has the same effect as applying it once; required because at-least-once delivery guarantees duplicates C. Operations that don't change state D. Operations that are idempotent by default in HTTP
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** In any at-least-once system (queues, retries, relay redelivery), duplicates *will* happen. Without idempotency you get double charges, double emails, double decrements. Prefer naturally idempotent operations (`SET x = 5`, not `x = x + 5`) and use idempotency keys for the rest.
Related: [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md) §7, [Ch. 07](07-message-queues.md) §3. </details>
**Q29. What does a saga give up compared to a two-phase commit?** A. Fault tolerance B. Atomicity and isolation — intermediate states are visible C. The ability to compensate D. Retryability
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** A saga is a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions. There's no all-or-nothing moment and no cross-step snapshot isolation, so intermediate states are visible and the UI must handle "payment pending, confirming shipment." In exchange you avoid 2PC's blocking and coordinator dependency.
Related: [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md) §8, [Ch. 08](08-distributed-primitives.md) §7. </details>
**Q30. Which data typically needs strong (linearizable) consistency?** A. Follower counts B. Account balances and payment status C. Feed rankings D. View counters
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Money must not be duplicated or lost. Follower counts, feed rankings, and view counters are all derived and eventually consistent without harm. Consistency is decided **per data class**, not system-wide.
Related: [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md) §1. </details>
**Q31. Why must consumers be idempotent?** A. To improve throughput B. Because at-least-once delivery means duplicates will occur C. To preserve ordering D. To enable parallel processing
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Producer retries, consumer crashes after processing but before acking, and relay redelivery all produce duplicates. An idempotent handler makes the *effect* exactly-once even though delivery isn't.
Related: [Ch. 07](07-message-queues.md) §3. </details>

**Q32. What's the best metric for "a consumer is falling behind"?** A. Messages processed per second B. Queue depth (number of unprocessed messages) C. Age of the oldest unprocessed message D. Consumer CPU usage
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**C.** Lag *count* is ambiguous — 1M messages might drain in seconds or represent days of backlog. Age is what users actually feel. (B is useful as a secondary signal; D tells you nothing about the backlog.)
Related: [Ch. 07](07-message-queues.md) §6. </details>

**Q33. How do you get per-key ordering in Kafka?** A. Increase the number of partitions B. Partition by the key so all events for a key land in one partition; consume partitions one at a time C. Use a single consumer group with many consumers D. Enable exactly-once semantics
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Ordering is guaranteed only *within* a partition. Partitioning by key routes a key's events to the same partition. The cost: a hot key concentrates all its traffic in one partition, capping its throughput at one consumer, and total parallelism is capped by the partition count.
Related: [Ch. 07](07-message-queues.md) §4, §8. </details>

**Q34. What should happen to a message that has failed repeatedly?** A. Retry forever B. Move to a dead letter queue and alert — don't auto-replay a poison message C. Drop it silently D. Route it to the primary queue again
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Infinite retries block the consumer forever. Auto-replaying a DLQ re-floods the queue with a message that will fail again. Instead: cap retries, dead-letter it with the original payload and error, alert on DLQ depth (a growing DLQ is a bug signal), and provide a selective replay tool with a "skip" option.
Related: [Ch. 07](07-message-queues.md) §5. </details>

**Q35. What's the difference between a queue and a log (Kafka)?** A. A log is faster B. A queue deletes messages after consumption; a log retains them, so each consumer group tracks its own offset and can replay C. A log doesn't support fan-out D. A queue supports exactly-once
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Kafka is a retained log, which gives you replay (rebuild a derived store from scratch), independent consumer groups, and both queue semantics (competing consumers in one group) and pub/sub (separate groups).
Related: [Ch. 07](07-message-queues.md) §2, §8. </details>

**Q36. What's the token bucket algorithm's key property?** A. It's strictly a fixed window B. It allows controlled bursts up to `burst` while the long-run average stays at `rate` C. It rejects requests when the queue is full D. It requires no shared state
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** A bucket holds up to `burst` tokens and refills at `rate`/sec; each request takes one token. This makes it the right choice for API gateways: it permits legitimate spikes without sustained overload.
Related: [Ch. 10](10-rate-limiting.md) §3.4. </details>
**Q37. Which HTTP response and header should a rate limiter return?** A. 503 with `Retry-After` B. 429 with `Retry-After` C. 400 with `Retry-After` D. 200 with `Retry-After`
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** 429 = "too many requests", and `Retry-After` tells the client exactly how long to wait. Without it, clients guess and often retry immediately, which defeats the limiter. Use 503 for "we're overloaded" (a different condition clients should handle differently).
Related: [Ch. 09](09-api-design.md) §7, [Ch. 10](10-rate-limiting.md) §6. </details>

**Q38. Why use a Lua script for a Redis rate limiter?** A. Lua is faster than Redis commands B. The token bucket needs a read-modify-write; Lua executes atomically so concurrent requests can't corrupt the count C. Redis requires Lua for TTLs D. Lua runs on the client
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Without a script, separate GET/HMSET commands can interleave under concurrency and lose updates. One Lua script runs atomically on the server.
Related: [Ch. 10](10-rate-limiting.md) §4.4. </details>
**Q39. The rate limiter's store is down. What should happen?** A. Always reject (fail closed) B. Always allow (fail open) with a local fallback limit C. Retry forever D. Route to a different region
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B** is the common answer: a limiter outage shouldn't take down the platform, and a local fallback prevents an unbounded flood. But it's a per-endpoint decision — fail **closed** for genuinely sensitive endpoints (signup, password reset, expensive AI calls). The important part is that you make the decision *explicitly* rather than by accident.
Related: [Ch. 10](10-rate-limiting.md) §4.3, §8. </details>

**Q40. Why is a concurrency limit often better than a rate limit for protecting a database?** A. It's simpler to implement B. A rate limit bounds requests/sec, but slow queries hold connections for seconds; a concurrency limit bounds in-flight work, which maps to connections and memory C. Concurrency limits allow more throughput D. Rate limits don't work on databases
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** The resource that matters is in-flight DB queries, not requests per second. A concurrency limit (semaphore) directly bounds connection pool usage.
Related: [Ch. 10](10-rate-limiting.md) §3.6, §10. </details>

**Q41. Why use content-hashed filenames instead of purging the CDN on deploy?** A. Hashed names are shorter B. A hash change produces a brand-new URL, so the CDN fetches it fresh with no purge — purges cost money, are slow, and aren't atomic across PoPs C. Purges aren't supported by CDNs D. Hashing compresses the content
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** The old URL stays cached but is no longer requested. This removes purges from the deploy path entirely — the most reliable CDN practice.
Related: [Ch. 11](11-cdn.md) §4.2. </details>

**Q42. What does `stale-if-error=86400` do?** A. Caches responses for 24 hours B. Serves a stale cached response for up to 24 hours if the origin errors C. Ignores origin errors for 24 hours D. Retries the origin for 24 hours
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** It converts an origin outage into degraded service. Combined with `stale-while-revalidate`, you keep serving users while the cache heals in the background.
Related: [Ch. 11](11-cdn.md) §3. </details>

**Q43. What's origin shielding?** A. Encrypting traffic between the CDN and the origin B. A tier of servers between the CDN and the origin, so a cache-miss storm doesn't hit the origin directly C. A firewall rule blocking direct origin access D. A second CDN in another region
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Without it, a viral asset or a purge causes every PoP to hit the origin simultaneously. With it, a couple of shield servers fetch once and serve all the PoPs.
Related: [Ch. 11](11-cdn.md) §9. </details>

**Q44. You serve per-user personalized HTML through a shared CDN cache. What's the danger?** A. It's slow B. If the cache key includes the user/session, each user gets their own entry, collapsing the hit rate; if the key doesn't, you serve one user's data to another C. The CDN can't store HTML D. It breaks TLS
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** The classic CDN personalization dilemma. Fixes: `Cache-Control: private` (no shared caching), or the **cached shell, dynamic hole** pattern — cache the shared page and fill user-specific fragments at the edge from a fast KV lookup.
Related: [Ch. 11](11-cdn.md) §2, §6. </details>

**Q45. Why should a `POST` endpoint accept an `Idempotency-Key`?** A. To make it faster B. Because POST isn't idempotent, and the client can't tell whether a timed-out request committed C. To compress the payload D. For HTTP caching
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** If a client times out, it doesn't know if the write landed. The idempotency key lets the server recognize a repeat and return the original response instead of executing again. The server stores `key → response` atomically with the effect.
Related: [Ch. 08](08-distributed-primitives.md) §4, [Ch. 09](09-api-design.md) §2. </details>

**Q46. Why is offset pagination risky on a large, actively-changing collection?** A. It's slow to compute B. Offsets are positions, not identities — inserts and deletes shift the window, so items get skipped or repeated; deep offsets also force a scan C. It doesn't support sorting D. It doesn't work with indexes
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Use cursor/keyset pagination (encode the last item's sort key) — stable and fast. For search, use `search_after` inside a Point in Time.
Related: [Ch. 09](09-api-design.md) §2. </details>

**Q47. Why must you validate the `alg` claim of a JWT?** A. To check the token isn't expired B. Because trusting the token's own `alg` allows `alg: none` and algorithm-confusion attacks that forge valid tokens C. To find the right signing key D. JWTs are always HS256
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Validate against a fixed allowlist of expected algorithms, check `exp`/`nbf`/`iss`/`aud`, and use constant-time signature comparison. Also remember: JWT payloads are only base64-encoded, never encrypted — don't put anything sensitive in them.
Related: [Ch. 09](09-api-design.md) §4. </details>

**Q48. What's the difference between 401 and 403?** A. 401 = not authenticated (get/refresh credentials); 403 = authenticated but not permitted (don't retry) B. 401 = server error; 403 = client error C. They are interchangeable D. 403 means the resource doesn't exist
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**A.** And a third: **404** — the resource doesn't exist (often returned instead of 403 to avoid confirming that someone else's resource exists).
Related: [Ch. 09](09-api-design.md) §2. </details>

**Q49. How do you evolve an API field's meaning without breaking clients?** A. Change it in place B. Expand-and-contract: add the new field, backfill, switch readers, stop writing the old, then remove it later C. Version the endpoint immediately D. Deprecate the old field with a header
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Clients running old code and servers running new code coexist during a rolling deploy, so every intermediate state must be valid. The general rule: **add fields, never remove or retype them**, and make clients ignore unknown fields.
Related: [Ch. 09](09-api-design.md) §3. </details>

**Q50. Why must a webhook verify both the signature and the timestamp?** A. It's redundant B. A signature proves authenticity but not freshness — without a timestamp check, a captured valid payload can be replayed later C. The timestamp is used to order events D. The signature is optional
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Also sign the **raw body** (JSON re-serialization changes the bytes and breaks the signature), and use a constant-time comparison. The receiver must still dedupe by delivery ID.
Related: [Ch. 09](09-api-design.md) §6. </details>

**Q51. What is an inverted index?** A. A map from document → terms B. A map from term → documents (with positions and frequencies), enabling fast full-text matching, scoring, and phrase queries C. A sorted list of documents by creation date D. A hash table of document IDs
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** It's the structure behind every search engine. A **forward** index (A) is the opposite and can't answer "which documents contain this term" efficiently.
Related: [Ch. 12](12-search.md) §2. </details>

**Q52. What does BM25's IDF term contribute?** A. It penalizes long documents B. It weights rare, discriminative terms far more than ubiquitous ones like "the" C. It handles synonyms D. It boosts recent documents
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** IDF = log(total docs / docs containing the term). Without it, every document scores highly on common terms and the ranking is meaningless. Length normalization is handled by the separate `b` parameter; recency decay isn't part of BM25 at all.
Related: [Ch. 12](12-search.md) §3. </details>

**Q53. How do you merge BM25 scores with vector similarity scores?** A. Add them directly B. Merge by rank, e.g. Reciprocal Rank Fusion, because the score scales aren't comparable C. Normalize to 0-1 and average — always correct D. Only use vectors for short queries
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** The two score distributions are completely different, so summing them is arbitrary. RRF (`score(d) = Σ 1/(k + rank_i(d))`) merges by rank. Then rerank the top ~100 candidates with a cross-encoder for precision.
Related: [Ch. 12](12-search.md) §3. </details>

**Q54. Why must authorization filters be applied inside the search query rather than after it?** A. Post-filtering is slower B. Post-filtering breaks result counts, pagination, and facet counts — and can leak whether a restricted document exists C. Elasticsearch doesn't support it D. It changes the score
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Facet counts and top-K are computed before filtering, so you get wrong counts, short pages, and an information leak. Use a `filter`/`term` clause on tenant or permission subjects.
Related: [Ch. 12](12-search.md) §9, §10. </details>

**Q55. What is mapping explosion?** A. A query returning too many results B. Dynamic mapping creating a new field per document, until the cluster has thousands of fields and dies C. Too many shards D. A slow bulk index
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Common with `json` fields containing random keys. Prevent with explicit mappings or `dynamic: strict`/`false`, and use `nested`/`flattened` for arbitrary keys.
Related: [Ch. 12](12-search.md) §6. </details>

**Q56. Why use presigned URLs for uploads instead of proxying through the API?** A. Presigned URLs are more secure B. The API server's memory, bandwidth, and threads become the bottleneck, and large uploads time out C. S3 requires it D. It reduces storage cost
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** The API should store *metadata*, not bytes. Constrain the presigned URL to a server-generated key, a content type, a length, and a short expiry — and never let the client choose the key.
Related: [Ch. 13](13-storage.md) §3. </details>

**Q57. What happens to orphaned multipart uploads?** A. They're cleaned up automatically by S3 B. They consume storage and are billed until aborted or expired — set a lifecycle rule C. They get merged into one object D. They fail with an error
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Always configure a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after a few days, and abort explicitly in your error paths.
Related: [Ch. 13](13-storage.md) §3.3. </details>

**Q58. Why store the file's bytes in object storage and the metadata in a database?** A. Object storage is required for large files B. Object storage is cheap and durable for blobs; a database is right for structured metadata, queries, and transactions. Mixing them makes both worse C. Databases can't store filenames D. It's a security requirement
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Blobs in a database bloat backups, pollute the buffer pool, slow vacuum, and explode replication traffic. Deleting a row doesn't promptly reclaim the space either.
Related: [Ch. 13](13-storage.md) §1, §8. </details>

**Q59. What's the main cost risk in a photo or video product?** A. CPU for image resizing B. Egress — media is served to every viewer while storage is paid once per file C. The number of database rows D. API requests to the CDN
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** This is why the CDN is the most important component in a media architecture: it cuts both latency and egress. Adaptive bitrate and long cache TTLs on immutable segments are the levers.
Related: [Ch. 11](11-cdn.md) §7, [Ch. 13](13-storage.md) §4. </details>

**Q60. What is a modular monolith?** A. A monolith with a microservice API in front B. One deployable unit with strict internal module boundaries, separate schemas per module, and communication through defined interfaces C. Several microservices sharing one database D. A monolith deployed in multiple regions
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** It's the right default: you get clear ownership and extraction seams without the distributed-systems tax. Enforce the boundaries with per-module schemas/permissions and CI checks.
Related: [Ch. 16](16-microservices.md) §2. </details>

**Q61. What is a bounded context?** A. A network boundary between services B. A DDD subdomain with its own model, rules, and language, within which the model is consistent C. A database schema D. A deployment boundary
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Services should map to bounded contexts — business capabilities — not to database tables or technical layers.
Related: [Ch. 16](16-microservices.md) §3. </details>

**Q62. Which is NOT a valid signal that your service boundaries are wrong?** A. Services are chatty — many calls per user request B. You need distributed transactions across them C. Services share database tables D. Services each have a single responsibility
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**D** is actually a *good* sign, not a bad one. A, B, and C all indicate the boundary is misplaced: chattiness means it's too fine, distributed transactions mean it splits a single business operation, and shared tables mean the boundary isn't real.
Related: [Ch. 16](16-microservices.md) §3. </details>

**Q63. What is the difference between a domain event and a command?** A. A domain event is a request; a command is a fact B. A domain event announces a fact that happened (past tense); a command requests a specific action with one intended handler C. They're the same thing D. Events are synchronous; commands are asynchronous
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Events decouple (many subscribers, each deciding what to do); commands couple explicitly (one handler, a clear intent).
Related: [Ch. 16](16-microservices.md) §4. </details>

**Q64. How do services read each other's data?** A. Direct database queries to the owning service's tables B. Via the owner's API, published events + local read models, or a shared read store C. By sharing a single schema D. They don't
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Each service owns its data exclusively; cross-domain reads go through an API (real-time) or via events into a local read model (eventual). Direct table access has no contract, no isolation, and breaks silently.
Related: [Ch. 16](16-microservices.md) §5. </details>

**Q65. What's the difference between an SLI, an SLO, and an SLA?** A. They're interchangeable B. SLI = the measurement, SLO = the target, SLA = the external contract with consequences C. SLI = the target, SLO = the contract, SLA = the measurement D. SLA is internal, SLO is external
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Typically SLI (e.g. "proportion of successful requests") → SLO (99.9% over 30 days) → SLA (the contractual promise, looser, e.g. 99.5% with credits).
Related: [Ch. 14](14-observability.md) §5. </details>

**Q66. How do you calculate the error budget for a 99.9% SLO?** A. 99.9% of requests B. 0.1% of requests over the window (about 43 minutes of downtime in 30 days) C. 1% of requests D. 43 minutes of requests
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Error budget = 1 − SLO = 0.1% of requests allowed to fail. Over a 30-day window that's ~43 minutes of total unavailability, or 0.1% of the requests in that window.
Related: [Ch. 14](14-observability.md) §6. </details>

**Q67. What is a burn rate of 14.4x, and what do you do about it?** A. The error rate is 14.4%; page immediately B. You're consuming the 30-day budget 14.4x faster than sustainable — about 2% of it in an hour; page C. Latency is 14.4x the baseline; create a ticket D. The service is at 14.4% CPU; scale up
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** A 14.4x burn consumes a 30-day budget in ~2 days, so it's urgent but not instantly fatal. The multi-window multi-burn-rate scheme pairs a long window (1h) with a short one (5m) to avoid flapping. Burn rate is a much better alerting signal than a raw error-rate threshold.
Related: [Ch. 14](14-observability.md) §6. </details>

**Q68. Why is `user_id` a terrible metric label but fine in a log?** A. It's fine in both B. Each distinct label value creates a separate time series, so millions of users would collapse the metrics backend; in logs it's just a field on a document C. Logs don't support filtering by user D. Metric labels are encrypted
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** This is the cardinality rule: never use unbounded values (user IDs, request IDs, timestamps, raw error messages) as metric labels. Use bounded enums, or put the detail in logs and traces.
Related: [Ch. 14](14-observability.md) §2. </details>

**Q69. Why page on symptoms rather than causes?** A. Symptoms are easier to measure B. Causes are often normal (high CPU is fine if latency is fine), and paging on them trains people to ignore pages C. Causes require more data D. Symptoms are more reliable
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Page when users are affected and a human must act. High CPU, queue depth, and disk usage belong on dashboards or in slow-burn tickets.
Related: [Ch. 14](14-observability.md) §7. </details>

**Q70. What is head sampling vs. tail sampling in tracing?** A. Head decides at the root span; tail decides after the trace completes. Tail keeps slow and failed traces that head would have discarded B. They're the same C. Head is for errors, tail is for spans D. Tail is cheaper
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**A.** Head sampling is cheap but loses slow/failed requests that happen to start in an unsampled trace. Tail sampling costs more (buffering) but retains exactly the traces you need for debugging. Tail is usually worth it.
Related: [Ch. 14](14-observability.md) §3. </details>

**Q71. What's the difference between RPO and RTO?** A. RPO is downtime, RTO is data loss B. RPO = max tolerable data loss (in time), RTO = max tolerable downtime C. They're identical D. RPO applies to databases, RTO to networks
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** They drive the architecture: RPO 0 forces synchronous replication; RTO 60 seconds forces automated failover with fast routing.
Related: [Ch. 15](15-reliability.md) §1. </details>

**Q72. What is a circuit breaker's HALF_OPEN state for?** A. Permanently blocking a dependency B. Letting a few probe requests through after the cooldown, to test recovery without flapping C. Increasing the timeout D. Reporting to the metrics system
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** OPEN fails fast; after a cooldown, HALF_OPEN admits a small number of probes — success closes the breaker, failure reopens it. Without HALF_OPEN, the breaker flaps between open and closed.
Related: [Ch. 15](15-reliability.md) §3.4. </details>

**Q73. Why does synchronous cross-region replication usually get rejected?** A. It's technically impossible B. It adds 50–150 ms to every write, destroying write throughput and latency C. It requires more storage D. It prevents backups
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** The standard answer is **sync within a region, async across regions**, with an explicit business-approved RPO (often 30 s to minutes). Synchronous cross-region is a business decision, not an engineering default.
Related: [Ch. 04](04-replication.md) §8, [Ch. 15](15-reliability.md) §5. </details>

**Q74. What's the benefit of cell-based architecture?** A. Lower per-request latency in all cases B. Blast-radius containment — a bug or outage in one cell affects only that cell's users C. It removes the need for a global router D. It guarantees strong consistency
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Cells also let you add capacity incrementally and run per-region cells for latency and data residency. The costs are cross-cell queries and routing complexity.
Related: [Ch. 15](15-reliability.md) §7. </details>
**Q75. What makes a backup real?** A. It's encrypted B. It's been successfully restored, on time, and verified C. It's stored in two places D. It runs automatically
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** An untested backup is a hypothesis. Do quarterly restore drills, measure the actual restore time against your RTO, and verify data integrity — not just that the file exists.
Related: [Ch. 15](15-reliability.md) §6. </details>

**Q76. You're at 100% DB CPU and 20% app-tier CPU. You add 50 app instances. What happens?** A. Latency improves B. Nothing improves and it gets worse — more concurrent queries hit an already-saturated DB, exhausting connections C. The DB scales automatically D. The cache absorbs it
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** You scaled the wrong tier. The fix is to reduce DB load (cache, read replicas, denormalization, async writes) or scale the DB. **Always name the bottleneck before scaling.**
Related: [Ch. 18](18-design-playbook.md) §6. </details>

**Q77. Which statement about "source of truth" is correct?** A. It's always the primary database B. It's the single place a fact is decided; everything else is derived and can be rebuilt C. It's the cache D. There's always exactly one per system
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** And "always the primary DB" is wrong — sometimes the authoritative source is an event log (event sourcing) or even a third party. There can be multiple source-of-truths, one per bounded context.
Related: [Ch. 00](00-foundations.md) §2, [Ch. 05](05-consistency.md) §1. </details>

**Q78. A service calls 3 independent dependencies, each with p99 = 40 ms, and the total budget is 150 ms. How should you call them?** A. Sequentially — 120 ms total, plus overhead, near the limit B. In parallel — total ≈ 40–50 ms C. Sequentially with caching D. In parallel with hedged requests on all three
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** Call them in parallel. Never stack p99s of independent operations — a parallel set's p99 approximates the slowest member's p99, not the sum. (D adds load you don't need here; hedging is for the tail when the p99 itself is the problem.)
Related: [Ch. 00](00-foundations.md) §5. </details>

**Q79. What's the most important sentence to say in a system design interview?** A. "I'll use Kafka and Redis." B. "The source of truth is X; everything else is derived. At 10x, Y saturates first, so here's the migration." C. "This is a well-known scalable pattern." D. "We'll use microservices."
<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B.** It demonstrates the three things you're actually being scored on: where authority lives, where the bottleneck is, and that you think about evolution. Technology choices are the least interesting part.
Related: [Ch. 22](22-interview-playbook.md) §11. </details>

**Q80. A deployment must support zero downtime. What's the correct sequence?** A. Replace all instances at once, then check health B. Mark instances drained (readiness false), wait for in-flight requests to complete, SIGTERM, wait for graceful shutdown, verify health, continue in batches — keeping a full batch serving C. Restart the primary database first D. Deploy during a traffic trough with no checks
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
**B.** Replacing all instances at once drops all capacity. Roll in batches (~10%) with draining and health verification, keeping at least one batch serving throughout.
Related: [Ch. 01](01-scaling.md) §5. </details>
